title: Pearls on a thread
hookLine: chapter seven opens with a sobering number, then strings the whole world on God like pearls on a thread
carry: the world is strung on God like pearls
last: TATA — NO GOOD EFFORT IS LOST, EVEN ACROSS LIFETIMES.

lines: THE THREAD WAS THERE ALL ALONG.
cards: A pearl necklace breaks, and the pearls scatter across the floor. For a second you see what was hidden the whole time: a thread running through every one of them, holding the shape.
You never noticed the thread, because the pearls were the pretty part. Still in the chariot between the two armies, Krishna opens chapter seven of the Gita with two things.
A sobering number about how rare real understanding is. And this very picture: the whole world, strung like pearls on a thread you can't see.

teach.b: Krishna opens by promising something complete. Listen, he says, and you'll know me fully, with jnana and vijnana: knowing about, and knowing through experience. Then the number, verse three.
Among thousands of people, one strives for perfection. And among those who strive and succeed, scarcely one knows me as I really am.
It's not a threat; it's honesty about how hard this is. Then he describes how the world is made.
There's his lower nature, eightfold: earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect, and the sense of I. That's everything you can point to, including your own thoughts.

And there's his higher nature, the life in things, which holds the whole world up. From these two, all beings come, and Krishna is the source and the end of the whole universe. Then verse seven, the necklace.
There is nothing higher than me, Arjuna.
All this is strung on me, like pearls on a thread. And he lists where the thread shows. I am the light of the sun and the moon.
The sacred syllable Om in all the Vedas. The sound in space. The sweet fragrance of the earth.

The strength of the strong, free of craving. This is the plainest picture of what Hindus mean by God in everything: not a God far above the world, but the thread through it. It's why many offer water to the rising sun.
Rare to see. But it runs through every pearl.

how: Hindus often chant Om at the start of prayer or study, and the image of the world strung on the divine like pearls on a thread (Gita 7.7) is a common teaching of God's presence in all things.

o: knowing by experience, not just facts

games.q: what's inside the chapter — tap the pairs.

s: Krishna says most seekers come to know him fully
verse 3: among thousands one strives, and of those scarcely one knows him truly.
mind and intellect are part of the lower nature in chapter seven
the eightfold lower nature includes mind, intellect and the sense of I.
the Gita says the thread is easy to see
verse 3 says scarcely one knows him as he really is.

games.q: Krishna lists eight parts of his lower nature: earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect, and one more. which?
games.why: the sense of I, ahamkara. even your sense of being a separate someone belongs to the lower nature; the higher nature is the life that holds the world up.

practice: Count through the eight of the lower nature, slowly, one per breath: earth, the weight of your body on the seat; water, the wet of your mouth; fire, the warmth of your hands; air, the breath itself; space, the room around you; mind, the thoughts passing; intellect, the part that's following along; and the sense of I, the one sitting here.
Then, for the rest of the time, rest on whatever holds all eight together.

wordCard.voice: Vijnana. Realization, knowing through experience, not just about. Gita seven, three: among thousands, one strives, and among those, scarcely one knows the truth. Rare, and still strung through everything.

orig.note: Sanskrit: sutre mani-gana iva, 'like clusters of gems on a thread' (7.7).

carryVoice: Your line: the world is strung on God like pearls. The light of the sun, the smell of the earth: the thread runs there too. Day one hundred eighty-three.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 7.4–7.7 (lower and higher nature; pearls on a thread)
